q7.answer: The API server generates the raw token in flow A and puts it in the queued reset job payload ({email, raw token}). The email worker reads the job and builds APP_URL/reset?token=<raw> into the email. Only the hash goes to Postgres. I did not check the queue's transport details.

q8.answer: The server hashes the token from the URL with SHA-256 and looks up the row in password_reset_tokens by token_hash (unique, indexed). It is good if consumed_at is null and expires_at is in the future; otherwise it shows the expired page [E]. The GET changes nothing.

q9.answer: There is no separate counter. The count is the number of rows in password_reset_tokens for that user with created_at within the last hour, counted inside the request transaction after locking the user row. Old requests drop out because they fall outside the created_at window. Rows are kept after expiry so the count stays correct.

q10.answer: Inside the request transaction, after the rate-limit check passes and before inserting the new row, all of the account's earlier unused tokens get consumed_at set to now. This happens before commit, so the old links die at the same moment the new one appears.

q11.answer: In one transaction: the token is marked consumed, the users password_hash is updated, and all of that user's sessions rows are deleted. The 'password changed' email is enqueued after the commit, not inside the transaction.

q12.answer: The submit transaction runs an UPDATE on the token row SET consumed_at=now WHERE hash matches AND consumed_at IS NULL AND expires_at>now, RETURNING user_id. The database lets only one of the racing submits update the row; the other gets 0 rows, rolls back and sees the expired page [E]. The earlier read check is just for a friendly error.
